data.question: Should the operator send R1 to the regulator, lowering vote.quorum from 2 to 1 only for this period's measured proposal 1 (block_k 3 → 2), or keep constitution-v1 unchanged?
data.background: R1 changes a value of the constitution (vote.quorum), which is a regulation-level change: only the regulator can make it, and it affects A, B, C and the customers. Under the current quorum, proposal 1 fails because B and C vote against it. R1 would change that vote outcome, so it would override two companies' votes. This is a trade between customer outcomes and the companies' voting rights that I must not settle myself.

options.summary: Lower vote.quorum 2 → 1, scoped to this period's measurement, so proposal 1 (block_k 3 → 2) passes on A's vote alone. Measured effect of proposal 1: on-time 216.6 → 223.8 (+7.2, 5/5 seeds); late 11.4 → 4.2; lowest on-time rate 0.93 → 0.97; worst_company_p95_wait_s 158 → 109; unfinished stays 0.0; blocked s 1824 → 936. Costs: road violations 19.0 → 28.0; utility B 68.5 → 65.5; utility C 65.8 → 56.3.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain: more on-time deliveries, fewer late ones, a higher floor for the worst-served company's customers, and shorter worst-case waits. A gains in utility (69.8 → 73.4) and its vote prevails. B and C lose utility and have their votes overridden on this proposal; C loses about 14%. If the scope does not hold in practice, every company, A included, could lose its veto on future amendments. Other road users may bear the risk from about 9 more road violations, whose safety relevance has not been diagnosed.

options.summary: Stay at constitution-v1 with quorum 2. Proposal 1 stays rejected (A for, B and C against) and the town stays at on-time 216.6, late 11.4, lowest on-time rate 0.93, worst_company_p95_wait_s 158 and road violations 19.0. Proposal 2 (hold_limit 60s → 50s) would also fail on C's vote; it gains only +0.4 on-time on 2/5 seeds.
options.stakeholders: Customers forgo about 7.2 on-time deliveries per period and keep the higher number of late deliveries; the worst-served company's customers stay at a 0.93 on-time rate. B and C keep their current utility and their veto. A forgoes its gain. Other road users keep the lower violation level. This is the third period in which this customer cost is accepted.

recommendation.reason: Proposal 1 meets the condition the operator set in D2. It passes check and the constitution, improves the main goal on all 5 seeds, and satisfies every KPI condition. It has now shown the same customer gain across repeated periods. The KPI explicitly allows proposing a regulation revision when votes block amendments that are good for customers. R1 is now framed as narrowly scoped and conditional on this period's measurement, not as a blanket cut. I recommend sending it to the regulator with this impact statement, but only if the regulator can bind its scope to proposal 1 (or to proposals that pass all KPI conditions on all seeds). If that binding is not possible, keep is the right choice. The unexplained rise in road violations and C's utility loss should be stated to the regulator as open risks.
assumptions: The regulator can technically limit the quorum change to proposal 1 or to proposals meeting the operator's D2 criteria, so that it does not become a general quorum of 1.
Next period's demand and conditions resemble the measured period, so the +7.2 on-time gain carries over.
The increase in road violations from 19.0 to 28.0 does not represent a material safety hazard to other road users.
B and C will keep operating normally and will not respond strategically (for example by withdrawing service) after being outvoted.

unknowns: Whether the regulator can legally and technically bind the quorum change to a narrow scope, or whether it would in effect become a general quorum of 1.
Which road violations increase under block_k 2 and whether they matter for the safety of other road users.
Why C loses about 14% of its utility, and whether that loss reaches C's customers in ways not captured by the town-wide metrics.
How B and C will act after being outvoted: future votes, service levels and possible strategic amendments.
How customers perceive the change and whether they value the on-time gain as the metrics suggest.
Next period's demand and whether the gain holds beyond 5 seeds and the measured conditions.
Whether a rule alternative exists that achieves similar customer gains while B and C would accept it.
